item.title: The bridge between science and policy: How IPBES redefined global conservation policy and its path to societal impact | Science
item.description: Global policy around climate and nature goals has evolved considerably over the last decade. Today, countries recognize that climate and biodiversity crises are profoundly interconnected, and that one cannot be solved without addressing the other. Elevating biodiversity and ecosystem collapse to the same geopolitical urgency as climate change is largely due to the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES). As the platform enters its second decade, and with the Convention on Biological Diversity Subsidiary Body on Implementation meeting in Nairobi this month to assess progress toward implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF), focus will be on how countries integrate IPBES assessment findings into their national policy and legislation frameworks, planning, and national budgets for a truly deep societal and institutional transformation.

item.title: Curb plastic pollution at its source | Science
item.description: Global plastic production has more than doubled since 2000 to roughly 460 million tonnes per year, about half of it destined for single-use products (1). After accounting for reprocessing losses, only about 9% of plastic waste is ultimately recycled, whereas nearly half is landfilled, about a fifth is incinerated, and the rest is mismanaged or leaks into ecosystems (1, 2). As governments negotiate a legally binding global plastics treaty (3, 4), they should recognize that recycling alone cannot solve plastic pollution and prioritize reducing production and reusing materials.

item.title: Dengue vaccines need long-term surveillance | Science
item.description: On 8 June, Brazil temporarily suspended its Butantan-DV dengue vaccination rollout after reports of rare and unexpected adverse events during early implementation (1–3). This decision—an appropriate response to a safety signal—should not be interpreted as evidence that dengue vaccination has failed. Rather, it serves as a call to make dengue vaccine deployment more scientifically accountable. Every dengue vaccine rollout should be paired with active pharmacovigilance, transparent reporting, and postlicensure studies that can distinguish vaccine-related adverse events from severe dengue occurring after vaccination. The priority is not to retreat from dengue vaccination but to ensure that safety, effectiveness, and serotype-specific performance are monitored in real time.
